description: A machine-sewn pieced wool U.S. flag with four grommets on the heading, 47 x 105 inches, stars in an 7-7-6-7-7- pattern, inscribed on the heading "Capt. Saml J. Hopkins, 7th N.J. Hopkins, 7th NJ Vol. Inf., 1862-1863; acquired by Calvin Bullock, circa 1930s, until passing, 1944; by descent to daughter of Hugh Bullock; purchased for the Zaricor Flag Collection by private treaty, New York City, 1997. Literature Bullock, Calvin. Sixty Years. New York, 1954. P 32. Exhibition The American Flag: Two Centuries of Concord & Conflict. First and Second Presidio Exhibits, Jan-Feb and May-July 2003. The Zaricor Flag Collection research suggests that this 34-star U.S. flag may have been made under contract to the State of New Jersey by William J. Yard of Trenton as part of a group of flags for use by recruiters endeavoring to fill the ranks of New Jersey's volunteer forces during the Civil War. The inked inscription on the canvas heading indicates that this particular flag was used by Captain (later Lt. Col.) Samuel J. Hopkins (1818-1881) of the 7th New Jersey Volunteer Infantry in his effort to recruit volunteers in 1862 and 1863. During the American Civil War the brass grommet, patented a decade before, found major use among flag-makers for the first time. Until the mass production of the brass grommet began, ties were run through whip-stitched buttonhole eyelets in the canvas or linen headings along the hoist edge of a flag, or a rope with toggle and loop were sewn directly into the heading. Although the brass grommet was a superior method of affixing halyards to flags, it was not universally adopted for another 25 years, and it was not available in the South at all during the Civil War.

title: Hand-sewn wool U.S. Flag with sewn cotton stars, 180 x 252 inches, canton 98 x 104 inches, white hoist, stars in 3-5-4-5-4-5-2,
description: Hand-sewn wool U.S. Flag with sewn cotton stars, 180 x 252 inches, canton 98 x 104 inches, white hoist, stars in 3-5-4-5-4-5-2, in poor condition, separated vertically, and with loss throughout. Provenance Fortress Monroe, Virginia, 1820s to 1860s; acquired and retained by Union Army Paymaster Major Eliphalet Rowell, as a memento of service until 1899; by donation to the Lowell Museum in Hallowell, Maine, until 1987; sold via James D Julia Auction House, Fairfield, ME to John Ockerbloom of Kittery Maine, 2004; sold by John Ockerbloom Kittery Maine via Amoskeag Auction House, of Manchester, New Hampshire, to Zaricor Flag Collection, 2004. Exhibitions Lowell Museum, Hubbard Free Library, Hallowell, Maine, circa 1899 to 1987. A "CONVERSION FLAG," WITH STARS ADDED TO KEEP IT CURRENT. This large wool garrison flag is an enigma. The flag has been torn vertically into two irregular pieces, making accurate identification difficult. It was previously identified as a flag from the 1837 -1846 period when U.S. flags had between 26 and 28 stars; however, there are inconsistencies in the star field that suggest it was originally made with fewer stars, and added to as more states entered the union. A close examination of the overall star design and the stitching in the seven rows of stars makes it clear that the bottom row of stars and possibly some in the top rows were added after the original manufacture. They are asymmetrical when compared to the stars in the second through fifth rows in the body of the canton. For the above-mentioned reasons, it is likely that this flag was originally a 23 star flag, with a 5-4-5-4-5 starfield, originally dating from1820-1821, and the other stars added later to keep the flag current. While the ultimate star count is still theoretical, the flag currently possesses 27 complete stars and traces of a 28th star in the top row of the canton, indicating that the tear occurred during its representation as a 28-star flag. The flag is rent in two, and there is a discoloration or a soiled appearance on the fly portion of the torn pieces, suggesting that the flag was flying from a free-standing pole when the tear took place. This tear was perhaps caused by severe weather conditions such as a hurricane. One such storm struck the fortress in 1845, during a visit from President & Mrs. John Tyler, when the 28-star flag was current. Another similar storm struck on 8 September 1846, also during the tenure of the 28-star flag. The "Fortress Monroe Flag" was for many years displayed in the historical collections of the Lowell Museum of the Hubbard Free Library in Hallowell, Maine, donated to that institution by Union Army Paymaster Major Eliphalet Rowell. During this time, it was identified by a paper label inscribed, "Fortress Monroe Flag." Fort Monroe, the "Gibraltar of the Chesapeake," was established at "Point Comfort," the site of the landing of the first enslaved Africans in English North America. It was a pivotal point of security throughout US history. Major Eliphalet Rowell (1822-1903) was a Hallowell, ME native who served as paymaster in the Civil War before returning to newspaper publishing in his post-war career.  In his obituary, published in the Kennebec Journal November 5, 1903, he is described as "A man of greatness and ennobling influences, and characteristic righteousness ... of noble instincts and unswerving rectitude."

description: A Quiet Afternoon oil on canvas 25 1/4 x 36 1/2 in. (64.1 x 92.7 cm) framed 35 x 46 1/4 x 3 1/4 in. (88.9 x 117.5 x 8.3 cm) Painted circa 1850.
provenance: Private collection, Mount Vernon, Maine. | Vose Gallery, Boston, acquired from the above, June 1972. | [With] Timken Museum of Art, San Diego, California, loaned from the above, 1972. | Vose Gallery, Boston, returned from the above, 1972. | Sale, Bourne Auction, Hyannis, Massachusetts, September 1974, sold by the above. | Private collection, Manchester, Massachusetts, 1974. | Edward Luke Stone and Cassandra (née Reeve) Stone, Newport, Rhode Island, acquired at the above sale. | [With] Vose Gallery, Boston, consigned from the above, July 2006. | Edward Luke Stone and Cassandra (née Reeve) Stone, Newport, Rhode Island, returned from the above, September 2006. | Cassandra (née Reeve) Stone, Newport, Rhode Island, by descent from the above, April 26, 2013. | Acquired by the present owner from the above, 2022. | | Around 1835, inspired by the Hudson River School master Thomas Cole (1801-1848) and with the patronage of the prominent New York merchant and art patron Luman Reed (1785-1836), Asher B. Durand ended a successful career as an engraver to dedicate himself to painting full time. In 1837 he accompanied Cole on a sketching trip to the Schroon Lake region in the Adirondacks, which led to Durand completing nine landscapes; these were exhibited at the annual National Academy of Design exhibition the same year. In 1838 and 1839, he again made summer sketching trips and contributed landscapes to subsequent Academy exhibitions. | | In the summer of 1840 Durand joined fellow artists John F. Kensett (1816-1872), John W. Casilear (1811-1893), and Thomas P. Rossiter (1818-1871) in Europe, where he studied the works of the Old Masters, especially Claude Lorrain (1600-1682). After his return to New York in July 1841, he exhibited paintings of European scenery, but soon resumed sketching tours in the Catskills and the Hudson River Valley during the summer. In 1845, Durand was named president of the National Academy, a position he would hold until 1861. He increasingly believed that directly studying nature should be the primary inspiration for American artists and began producing meticulously painted works that were admired for their faithful depictions of natural forms, light and atmosphere. Such works also expressed sentiments similar to those in the poetry of his friend William Cullen Bryant. Several of his paintings of the 1850s were directly inspired by Bryant's poems. | | In 1847, a critic for the New York Evening Post discussed Asher B. Durand's work alongside Thomas Cole, praising, "It is now generally conceded, we believe, that Cole and Durand are the two most prominent landscape painters in this country. They are indeed artists of superior ability and will undoubtedly hereafter be looked upon as the founders of two American schools. Each one is distinguished for peculiar excellencies...Cole has a passion for the wild and tempestuous; Durand is a lover of the cultivated country when glowing in mellow sunlight." (L.S. Ferber, Kindred Spirits: Asher B. Durand and the American Landscape, exhibition catalogue, New York, 2007, p. 161) | | Following Cole's death in 1848, Durand solidified a leading role in the American landscape school and exerted considerable influence on many younger painters. His Kindred Spirits of 1849 (Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art), painted in memory of Cole, almost immediately became one of the best-known paintings in the country and continues to be one of the top examples of early American landscape painting to this day. | | Durand continued to sketch in the summers and paint in New York during the winters throughout his artistic career. As the ever-increasing pressures of the Industrial Revolution came to bare, Americans sought refuge in the tranquility of pastoral scenes such as Durand's A Quiet Afternoon. The glorification of nature was never more important to a society struggling with the rapid expansion of their country. Here he uses a softness in his brushwork, much like the paintings of Claude Lorrain, to emphasize the solitude of the scene. Oswaldo R. Roque wrote, "The effect of the success of Durand's style was to push American landscape painting further toward nature and away from man. His broader attitude to what was picture-worthy in nature and his assertion that attentiveness to nature's details was the only way of arriving at the truth were of vast import. His approach, of course, was productive of a realism that in subsequent years was taken to be his major contribution to the Hudson River School." (American Paradise: The World of the Hudson River School, New York, 1987, p. 37) |

This is the setting copy with printer's markings in the text, including a notation at the upper right corner of the first page, next to the title: " July St. Nic ... Wanted soon, by May 4th " The story was published in St. Nicholas magazine, volume XI, number 8, July 1884, and was later included in the collection Spinning-Wheel Stories . Jerseys is perhaps the most important of her Spinning Wheel Stories , a collection of often polemical narratives. An early feminist, Alcott introduces the latest concepts of late 19th Century dress and diet reform. Not every student at Madame Stein's Select Boarding School welcomes the new teacher's radical principles. "I do hope Miss Orne isn't full of the new notions about clothes, and food, and exercise, and rights and rubbish of that sort," complains narrow minded Maude. "Mamma hates such ideas, and so do I." Despite initial resistance to her instruction, Miss Orne's experiment proves in the end to be a great success in the preparation of healthy young lives. No other important Louisa May Alcott manuscript for a work of fiction has come up for auction in nearly forty  years. See Eiselein and Phillips, The Louisa May Alcott Encyclopedia , p 158; Stern 228 and 234.

provenance: Property from the Historic Collection of William Russell Shaw. | | Provenance Note | Although Shaw married in 1792, he died without issue. His possessions with restrictive covenants favoring eldest male descendants, including the family Bible and hereditary rights to membership in the Society of the Cincinnati, passed to his nephew, Robert Gould Shaw (1776-1853), and then to Robert's eldest son, Francis George Shaw (1809-82), who married another of Samuel's descendants, Sarah Blake Sturgis Shaw (1815-1902). Their only son, Colonel Robert Gould Shaw (1837-63), was killed in action while leading the first Black volunteer regiment of the U.S. Army in an assault on Fort Wagner, South Carolina. (The motto of the Society of the Cincinnati is inscribed above Shaw's likeness in Augustus Saint-Gaudens' Memorial to the 54th Massachusetts Regiment on Boston Common, completed in 1897). The medal thus passed to nephew George Russell Shaw (1848-1937), who was a prominent architect in Boston and Concord, Massachusetts. In addition to the insignia, George inherited a caudle cup and saucer from Samuel Shaw's own Cincinnati porcelain service, which were purchased by Henry Francis du Pont in the early 1930s and are now in the collection of Winterthur Museum, Delaware, (acc. no. 1953.166.1-.2). The medal thereafter passed by descent through the eldest son to consignor. | | Biographical Note | Born and raised in Boston, Massachusetts, Samuel Shaw (1754-94) enlisted in the Continental Army at Cambridge in 1775 and rose to the rank of Major before its dissolution in early 1784. By war's end, Shaw had become aide-de-camp to Washington's chief of artillery, Major General Henry Knox (1750-1806), and assisted him in establishing the Society of the Cincinnati at West Point on 13 May 1783. An international fraternal organization for Revolutionary War officers and their descendants, the Society counts George Washington, Alexander Hamilton, Aaron Burr, and the Marquis de Lafayette among its founding members. Its earliest medals, diplomas, and porcelain services bear insignia designed by Pierre Charles L'Enfant (1754-1825), the first city planner for Washington, DC. | | During his subsequent career in the China and East India trade, Shaw distinguished himself as "the central character in the story of the Cincinnati porcelain."* In 1784, within months of his discharge from the Army, Shaw departed New York Harbor as supercargo on The Empress of China, the first U.S. merchant vessel to trade in Canton (Guangzhou). Whether acting on instructions or independently, Shaw came prepared to commission "something emblematic of the institution of the order of the Cincinnati executed upon a set of porcelain."** As was customary, he engaged an enamel painter at Canton to add custom decoration to objects shaped and fired at the inland factories in Jingdezhen. Shaw described his vision for the Society porcelain in his journal: "the American Cincinnatus, under the conduct of Minerva, regarding Fame, who, having received from them the emblems of the order, was proclaiming it to the world." He provided the painter with "two separate engravings of the goddesses, an elegant figure of a military man, and...a copy of [L'Enfant's] emblems." The result is displayed on the first Cincinnati porcelain sold in the United States, a 302-piece service purchased by George Washington and now in collections of Mount Vernon, the Society of the Cincinnati, and the Metropolitan Museum of Art, among others. It was likely on Knox's recommendation that Washington appointed Shaw the first U.S. Consul to China in 1786, a title Shaw maintained up until his death on a return voyage from Canton and Bengal in 1794. | | *Lindsay E. Borst, "The Society of the Cincinnati Chinese Export Porcelain," Cincinnati Fourteen 48/2 (Spring 2012): 14-23. | **Josiah Quincy, The Journals of Major Samuel Shaw, the First American Consul at Canton, with a Life of the Author (Boston: William Crosby and H.P. Nichols, 1847).

description: John Johnston (1753-1818), Boston, Massachusetts, c. 1790 Shaw, wearing a powdered wig and yellow vest, sits in three-quarter profile against an archway looking out on a three-masted merchant ship at sea flying two American flags; he writes with a quill pen at a desk, surrounded by a standish, loose papers, and the books Guthrie's Geography and East India Directory against the wall; mounted in a later carved and gilded frame. The ship in the background has not been positively identified. Some claim it to be The Empress of China , and others suggest it is Shaw's own ship, the Massachusetts , which at 800 tons was the largest American merchant vessel yet built when it sailed for Canton (Guangzhou) in March 1790. Sold with custom box on chest containing a leather-bound King James Bible published by John Baskerville of Cambridge, England, in 1763. Thomas Freeman, a manager for the English East India Company at Canton, presented the Bible to Shaw on New Year's Day, 1791, as noted on the first of six manuscript leaves tipped into the front. The gift inscription stipulates that the book serve as a family register, passed through the eldest male descendants. Each of the subsequent tipped-in leaves are inscribed with genealogical records traced back to colonial ancestor John Shaw (1618-89) and updated through 1990. An especially poignant entry appears on the sixth page, reading: Robert Gould Shaw, born 10 October, 1837 (only son of Francis George and Sarah Blake Shaw), to whom had he survived his father, this Book would have passed in direct descent, was killed the 18th of July A.D. 1863, on the parapet of Fort Wagner, in the harbor of Charleston, So. Ca., leaving no child. In April 1861, at the President's first call for volunteers, he [became] a private in the ranks of the 7th Reg't New York State Militia; in March of the same year, he joined the 2nd Massachusetts Volunteer Regiment as 2nd Lieut., and remained with it, participating in its battles and rising to the rank of Captain, till, early in (February) 1863, he was deemed worthy to be commissioned as Colonel of the Fifty-fourth (54th) Massachusetts Regiment, the first colored Regiment raised in any of the Free States. He was shot through the heart as he led the assault on Fort Wagner at the head of his men, and was buried, with many of his brave and devoted followers, by the enemy, in the ditch of the Fort. He was loved and honored by all who knew him. He devoted himself to the common cause of our beloved Country and of all Mankind. His life was pure and noble, his death glorious. / (Written by his Father, 1 August 1863). Thus, the Bible passed to eldest nephew George Russell Shaw (1848-1937), a prominent Boston architect and an early patron of the Society of Arts & Crafts in that city, specializing in leatherwork and bookbinding together with his wife, Emily Mott Shaw (1848-1927). description: Panoramic Landscape with a Ruined Tower signed and dated 'Louis R. Mignot 1852' (lower right) oil on canvas 28 3/8 x 35 7/16 in. (72.5 x 90.5 cm) framed 35 x 41 1/8 x 2 in. (89.0 x 107.0 x 5.0 cm)
provenance: A private Massachusetts collection. | | N.B. | The subject and style of the present picture align with what is known of Mignot's work during his six formative years as an aspiring artist at The Hague (1848-1854). Mignot's paintings from this period reflect his thorough study of the techniques and tropes of Dutch landscape practice, which he learned in the studio of Andrea Schelfhout (1787-1870), the most successful Dutch landscape painter of his day. Equally important was the example of 17th-century Dutch landscape art on view at the Mauritshuis and in other public and private collections. | | The present painting shares striking features with numerous paintings by Schelfhout, particularly Panoramic Landscape with Ruins, which is dated just two years before the present picture and while the artist was in Schelfhout's studio. This painting is almost certainly inspired by scenery much closer to home, however, such as Gelderland or possibly the Rhineland. | | The shepherd, his sheep, and the two peasant women (all stock characters of European picturesque scenery) are likely the work of a collaborator more skilled in figures. It was a common practice for landscape painters, including Schelfhout, to employ the services of figure painters to populate their scenes. Mignot entered into several such collaborations during his career. At about the same time he painted the present painting, Mignot collaborated with his friend and fellow American Eastman Johnson in the painting Doorway of a Castle in Winter (Manthorne/Coffey, no. 8). It's entirely possible that Johnson is also the uncredited figure painter in the present picture. | | While at The Hague, Mignot was perennially short of funds. He therefore resorted to shipping paintings back to New York and his hometown Charleston in the hope of exhibition and sales. (We have record of one painting bought by the American Art Union for distribution in 1850 and three paintings selected in 1853 for the annual exhibition of the National Academy of Design.) It seems probable that the present painting was also shipped to the United States and sold to an unidentified collector, only to resurface on the art market a century later. | | We would like to thank John W. Coffey for his kind assistance in authenticating and cataloguing this lot via the examination of digital images.

Victory , the Grand Dame of the Royal Navy, is a 104-gun first-rate ship of the line of the Royal Navy, ordered in 1758, laid down at Chatham Dockyard in 1759 and launched in 1765. In her long career she often served as Flagship, including Admiral Keppel's flagship at Ushant, Admiral Lord Howe's flagship at Cape Spartel and Admiral Jervis's flagship at Cape St Vincent. However, she is best known as Lord Nelson's flagship at the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805 which made her immortal. After 1824, she served as a harbor ship. In 1922, she was moved to a dry dock at Portsmouth, England and preserved as a museum ship. Since October 2012, she has been the flagship of the First Sea Lord and the world's oldest naval ship still in commission.

description: Paint Creek Herd , c. 1870 signed 'H. Dousa' (lower right); inscribed 'Paint Creek Herd Property of / Thomas and J.S. Kirk / Washington CH / Fayette C. Ohio' (lower left) oil on canvas 34 1/4 x 48 in. (87.0 x 121.9 cm) framed 40 1/4 x 54 1/4 x 2 1/2 in. (102.2 x 137.8 x 6.4 cm)
provenance: The ancestors of the current owner (acquired directly from the artist). | Then by descent. | To the collection of Grayson Louis Kirk (1903-1997). | The present private collection (by descent from the previous). | | N.B. | The details of Henry Dousa's life are relatively obscure. He was born in Germany and came to the United States in around 1860. He began working as a painter in the communities of Washington Court House and Mechanicsburg, Ohio, before going to Lafayette, Indiana, by 1885. He next appears in the records of the Saint Louis Post-Dispatch in 1894, and he likely died in Saint Louis within the following decade. | | Dousa is known particularly for his folk art paintings of farms and livestock in the Fayette County area, in which he would often inscribe the owners' and animals' names. Only around a dozen signed pictures by Dousa are known to exist, and this is an exciting and rare work - particularly considering its size and complexity - to come to auction. | | The present painting has been in the collection of the same family since it was painted. It depicts the cattle herd of Paint Creek Farm in Washington Court House, Fayette County, Ohio. Paint Creek Farm was started by the current owner's great-great-great-grandfather, James Kirkpatrick (d. 1840), an early settler who came to Ohio from Virginia in 1812. Upon James's death, the farm passed to his eldest surviving son, Thomas Kirk (born 1813). This picture was likely commissioned by Thomas and his son, also James, during Dousa's time in Ohio, when he would travel from place to place offering to paint the landowners' herds and farms. | | The picture identifies the farm's cattle herd (from left to right): Wabaunsee at 9 Years (A.H.B. Vol. 9th), Loudon Duke (No. 10400 A.H.B.), Cambridge Rose 3rd at 2 years (A.H.B. Vol. 12th), Lady Sheff 7th at 3 years (A.H.B. Vol. 12th), and Irene 15th at 5 years (A.H.B. Vol. 11th).

title: A pieced felt and rayon guidon, alternating yellow and red diagonal stripes, reading left to right "C / Animal / [bulldog] / Aggression / 4" with "USMC" lettered vertically on the fly end.
description: A pieced felt and rayon guidon, alternating yellow and red diagonal stripes, reading left to right "C / Animal / [bulldog] / Aggression / 4" with "USMC" lettered vertically on the fly end. Minor soiling and age toning. Provenance Vernacular WWII construction by unidentified U.S. Marines, 1942/44; acquired from estate of U.S. Marine by The War Museum, New York, 1980s; sold to Zaricor Flag Collection at auction, World War II: The Pacific Theater , sale 21082, Bonhams, New York (22 February 2013), lot 144. This unofficial guidon was likely used as an informal decoration to boost morale.  The inscription "animal aggression" paired with the head of a bulldog wearing a helmet references the USMC mascot, the "Devil Dog," a nickname attributed to German fighters who coined it after their first engagement with the USMC in 1918.  The 4th referred here could be the 4th Marine Raider Battalion (1942-44), the 4th Marine Regiment (disbanded 1942, reformed 1944) or, less likely, the 4th Marine Division (reserve division).

description: Gugler Lithographic Co., Milwaukee, Wisconsin, c. 1962 the well-preserved advertisement in twelve halftone screen-printed sheets retaining strong colors, particularly the brilliant red background, minor toning to edges only noticeable in margins, each paper sheet measures 59 inches tall and 43 inches wide, assembling to a full size of nearly 10 feet tall and 21.5 feet wide.
provenance: Possibly in storage at Gugler Lithographic Co. c. 1962-1976, then by descent to a Milwaukee collector. | | Note | Gugler Lithographic Co. was a Milwaukee fixture from 1878 onwards, where it was the primary producer for all of Pabst's advertising materials; at the time, Pabst was the largest brewer in the United States. Gugler lithography and printing was also responsible for the creation of WWII era war bond billboards, a classic lithograph of Abraham Lincoln, and the Beatle's White Album cover. | | The well-preserved condition of the advertisement owes to the fact that it was kept away from air and light from 1976-2003, at which point it was unfolded in a high-humidity environment to minimize creasing; it has been stored flat until present. | | The back of the first numbered sheet contains a diagram for assembly of the complete image, along with production information. The full image is titled "PABST BEER' NOW - NO DIRT ON CAN TOPS' and design number "DES.P-62". Each sheet is numbered "1162 PABST X", where x is the number of the panel in the overall design. Based on the numbering scheme and on the evolution of can design over the 1960s and 70s, we believe that the production year of this advertisement is very likely to be 1962.
